questions.q: Alkanes react with chlorine in ultraviolet light by:
questions.solution:
**Free radical substitution**, initiated by UV light splitting $\text{Cl}_{2}$ homolytically into two radicals.

The three stages are **initiation, propagation and termination**, and the propagation steps are what make one photon able to convert thousands of molecules.

**Electrophilic addition.** The $\pi$ electrons of the double bond are exposed and electron-rich, so they attract electrophiles.

The bromine molecule is **polarised** as it approaches, and adds across the double bond — which is why bromine water is decolourised.

questions.q: When HBr adds to propene, the major product is:
questions.solution:
**2-bromopropane** — Markovnikov's rule.

The reaction goes through the **more stable carbocation**, and a secondary cation is stabilised by two electron-releasing alkyl groups where the primary one has only one.

questions.q: Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition because:
questions.solution:
Addition would break up the **delocalised $\pi$ system** and lose the extra stability it confers — about $152$ kJ/mol.

**Substitution** leaves the ring intact, which is why benzene's chemistry is so different from an alkene's despite the apparent double bonds.
options: addition would destroy the delocalised system

questions.solution:
There are not enough hydrogens to saturate both fragments, so at least one must contain a **double bond**.

That is why cracking is the industrial source of alkenes, which crude oil itself barely contains.
options: a shorter alkane and an alkene

questions.q: How many structural isomers does pentane, $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{12}$, have?
questions.solution:
Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane — $\mathbf{3}$.

They differ markedly in boiling point: the more branched, the less surface contact and the weaker the van der Waals forces.

questions.q: Find the degree of unsaturation for $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6}$.
questions.solution: $\dfrac{2(6) + 2 - 6}{2} = \dfrac{8}{2} = \mathbf{4}$ — three from the double bonds and one from the ring. Benzene.

questions.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in an alkene with $5$ carbon atoms?
How many stereoisomers does but-2-ene have?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{2}$ — E (trans) and Z (cis).

The double bond cannot rotate, so the two arrangements cannot interconvert. But-1-ene has none, since one carbon of its double bond carries two identical hydrogens.

questions.q: Describe the mechanism of the chlorination of methane in three stages with equations, and explain why a mixture of products is obtained.
questions.solution:
**Initiation.** UV light breaks the Cl–Cl bond **homolytically** — one electron to each atom:

$\text{Cl}_{2} \xrightarrow{\;h
u\;} 2\text{Cl}\cdot$

Chlorine is chosen rather than methane because the Cl–Cl bond ($242$ kJ/mol) is much weaker than C–H ($412$).

**Propagation** — two steps that regenerate a radical, so the chain continues:

$\text{Cl}\cdot + \text{CH}_{4} \to \text{HCl} + \cdot\text{CH}_{3}$

$\cdot\text{CH}_{3} + \text{Cl}_{2} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}\cdot$

**The chlorine radical is back**, so one photon can convert thousands of molecules. This is what makes it a chain reaction.

**Termination** — any two radicals meeting:

$\text{Cl}\cdot + \text{Cl}\cdot \to \text{Cl}_{2}$

$\cdot\text{CH}_{3} + \cdot\text{CH}_{3} \to \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}$ (ethane, an unexpected by-product that is itself evidence for the mechanism)

$\cdot\text{CH}_{3} + \text{Cl}\cdot \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{Cl}$

**Why a mixture forms.** The product $\text{CH}_{3}\text{Cl}$ still has three C–H bonds, and a chlorine radical cannot tell it apart from methane. Further substitution gives $\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$, $\text{CHCl}_{3}$ and $\text{CCl}_{4}$.

**It is therefore a poor synthetic method** — the products are hard to separate. Using a large excess of methane favours the monosubstituted product, but nothing eliminates the problem.

The same chemistry, higher in the atmosphere, is how CFC radicals destroy ozone — one chlorine atom, regenerated indefinitely, taking thousands of ozone molecules with it.

questions.q: Describe the mechanism of the addition of HBr to propene, and use it to explain Markovnikov's rule.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the electrophile attacks.** The $\pi$ bond is a region of high electron density, and it attracts the $\delta+$ hydrogen of HBr.

The $\pi$ electrons form a bond to that hydrogen, and the H–Br bond breaks **heterolytically**, both electrons going to the bromine:

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}{=}\text{CH}_{2} + \text{HBr} \to \text{carbocation} + \text{Br}^{-}$

**Step 2 — the nucleophile attacks.** The bromide ion attacks the positively charged carbon, giving the product.

**Why the orientation is not random.** The proton can add to either carbon, giving either a **primary** or a **secondary** carbocation.

• Adding H to C1 leaves the positive charge on C2 — a **secondary** cation, flanked by two methyl groups.

• Adding H to C2 leaves it on C1 — a **primary** cation, with only one.

**Alkyl groups release electrons inductively**, spreading the positive charge and stabilising the cation. So the secondary cation is lower in energy and forms much faster.

**The major product is therefore 2-bromopropane**, and **Markovnikov's rule** — that the hydrogen adds to the carbon already carrying more hydrogens — is simply a shorthand for 'the more stable carbocation wins'.

**The order of stability is tertiary $>$ secondary $>$ primary**, and it explains far more than this one reaction: it is also why tertiary halides hydrolyse by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ and primary ones do not.

questions.q: Give the evidence for the delocalised structure of benzene, and describe the mechanism of its nitration.
questions.solution:
**The evidence against Kekulé's alternating double bonds.**

1. **Bond lengths.** X-ray diffraction shows all six C–C bonds are identical at $139$ pm — between a single ($154$) and a double ($134$). Kekulé's structure requires two different lengths.

2. **Enthalpy of hydrogenation.** Cyclohexene releases $120$ kJ/mol, so three isolated double bonds should release $360$. Benzene releases only $208$ — it is **$152$ kJ/mol more stable** than the Kekulé structure predicts.

3. **Chemical behaviour.** Benzene does not decolourise bromine water, and it undergoes **substitution** rather than addition — keeping the ring intact rather than destroying it.

4. Only **one** 1,2-disubstituted isomer exists, whereas alternating bonds would give two.

**The structure.** Each carbon contributes one electron in a $p$ orbital perpendicular to the ring; these overlap all the way round, forming a **delocalised $\pi$ cloud** above and below the plane.

**Nitration mechanism.**

**Generating the electrophile.** Concentrated sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water:

$\text{HNO}_{3} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \to \text{NO}_{2}^{+} + \text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+} + 2\text{HSO}_{4}^{-}$

**Attack.** The delocalised electrons attack $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$, giving an unstable intermediate in which the delocalisation is partly broken.

**Loss of a proton.** $\text{HSO}_{4}^{-}$ removes the H from the substituted carbon, **restoring the aromatic system** — which is the driving force for the whole second step.

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6} + \text{HNO}_{3} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4},\;55°\text{C}} \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Why $55$°C.** Hotter, and further nitration gives dinitrobenzene. The sulphuric acid is a **catalyst** and is regenerated.

Nitrobenzene is the gateway to aniline, and hence to dyes and pharmaceuticals.

questions.q: Explain why alkenes show E-Z isomerism but alkanes do not, state the conditions for it, and explain the E-Z naming rules.
questions.solution:
**Why alkenes do.** The C=C double bond consists of a $\sigma$ bond and a $\pi$ bond. Rotating about the bond would require breaking the $\pi$ overlap, which costs about $260$ kJ/mol — far more than is available at room temperature.

**The bond is therefore locked**, and the groups on either side are held in fixed relative positions.

**Why alkanes do not.** A C–C single bond is a $\sigma$ bond only, cylindrically symmetrical, so rotation is essentially free — millions of times a second. Any two arrangements interconvert instantly and are the same compound.

**The conditions for E-Z isomerism.**

1. A **C=C double bond** (or a ring, which is similarly rigid).

2. Each carbon of the double bond must carry **two different groups**.

If either carbon carries two identical groups, flipping the molecule gives the same thing. But-1-ene has none; but-2-ene has two isomers.

**The naming rules (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog).**

1. On each carbon, decide which group has **higher priority** — the one whose first atom has the greater **atomic number**.

2. If the first atoms tie, work outwards until they differ.

3. **Z** (*zusammen*, together) if the two higher-priority groups are on the **same** side; **E** (*entgegen*, opposite) if on opposite sides.

**Why E-Z replaced cis-trans.** With four different groups, 'cis' and 'trans' have nothing to refer to. E-Z always gives an unambiguous answer.

**The isomers are genuinely different compounds** with different melting points, dipole moments and biological activity — and in the case of retinal in the eye, the light-driven Z-to-E conversion is the first step of vision.

questions.q: Describe addition polymerisation, name three addition polymers with their uses, and discuss the disposal problem and its solutions.
questions.solution:
**The process.** Many alkene monomers join end to end with **no other product**. The $\pi$ bond opens and each unit bonds to the next:

$n\,\text{CH}_{2}{=}\text{CH}_{2} \to -\!\left(\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\right)_{n}\!-$

**Unsaturation is essential** — alkanes cannot polymerise this way. It also means the atom economy is $100\%$, since nothing is lost.

**Three polymers.**

• **Poly(ethene)** — bags, bottles, packaging. Low-density for film, high-density for rigid containers.

• **Poly(propene)** — ropes, crates, carpet fibres; stronger and with a higher melting point.

• **PVC** — pipes, window frames, cable insulation. Rigid alone, flexible with a plasticiser.

• **PTFE** — non-stick coatings, chemically inert.

**The disposal problem.** The saturated C–C backbone is **non-biodegradable**: no enzyme attacks it, so plastics persist for centuries in landfill and in the oceans, where **microplastics** have now entered the food chain.

Burning them releases carbon dioxide and, from PVC, toxic hydrogen chloride.

**The solutions, in order of preference.**

1. **Reduce** — the only measure that removes the problem rather than managing it.

2. **Reuse.**

3. **Recycle** — effective for a single sorted polymer, difficult for mixtures, which is why the recycling symbols number the types.

4. **Feedstock recycling** — cracking waste plastic back into monomers or into other useful chemicals.

5. **Biodegradable polymers** made from plant starch, or **photodegradable** ones with bonds that ultraviolet light will break.

The property that makes plastics so useful — that nothing attacks them — is precisely the property that makes disposing of them so hard.
